answer: Memory-hard minting resists sybils: each identity's mint evaluates a memory-hard function needing a large RAM block held for the whole computation, uncacheable across identities. Running N identities at once demands N times the memory simultaneously — a garden of fakes each needs its own full buffer, no sharing, because the access pattern forces distinct live memory. A grove of cheap parallel cores buys nothing when the binding cost is concurrent RAM per identity, so a reef of thousands of fakes must provision thousands of large buffers at the same instant.
